title: A daughter is better
hook: the king is disappointed at a daughter; the Buddha says she may do better than a son (SN 3.16)

segments.voice: Yesterday: four mountains rolling in on King Pasenadi, and your line, mountains closing in. What did you decide matters most? Today the same king gets news from home, and doesn't like it. Day six hundred forty-one.

King Pasenadi is sitting with the Buddha when a man comes in and whispers in his ear. Queen Mallika has given birth. A daughter. And the text, which rarely tells us what kings feel, says it plainly: the king was displeased. In his world, a son carried the throne, the family name, the rites for the ancestors. A daughter, many people thought, was a loss. Everyone at court would have understood the look on his face. The Buddha sees it, and says something nobody in that room expected. Today: a daughter is better.
screen: `A WHISPER IN THE KING'S EAR.` → `A DAUGHTER, AND HE'S DISPLEASED.` → `THE BUDDHA SEES HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: SN 3.16 is just the scene and one verse. The Buddha speaks to the king directly. A woman, lord of the people, may turn out better than a man. She may be wise and virtuous. And her son may become a hero, a ruler of lands. That's the whole teaching, and it's worth being honest about both halves of it. The first half is bold for its setting. In a court where the birth of a girl was met with a frown, the Buddha says, out loud, to the king himself, that a daughter may be better than a son. Better, not just as good. And he says why: wisdom and virtue, qualities of the person, not of the body. The second half speaks in the terms of its time. The verse praises her as a devoted wife who honors her husband's mother, and as the mother of a son who may rule. Those were the roles the king would recognize, and the verse meets him there. Modern readers often notice that tension, and Buddhist teachers today discuss it openly. Still, the verse was spoken to change a father's face. The sutta doesn't tell us what the king said next. Queen Mallika herself, the story's mother, appears elsewhere in the texts as a thoughtful follower of the Buddha, and tradition says she started life as the daughter of a garland-maker. A girl nobody expected much from, who became a queen. The birth that disappointed a king is, in a way, a story about her too.
screen: `A WHISPER: IT'S A DAUGHTER` · `SHE MAY TURN OUT BETTER` · `WISE AND VIRTUOUS, IN HER OWN RIGHT` · `SPOKEN IN THE TERMS OF ITS TIME` · then, large: `A DAUGHTER MAY BE BETTER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and remember something that arrived in your life and wasn't what you wanted. A job, a move, a change of plans, a person you didn't expect to matter. Notice the first reaction you had, the frown, the way the king frowned. Now look at what that thing became. Maybe it turned out better. Maybe it's still unfolding. Either way, breathe, and let a little room open around it. Practice welcoming the unexpected with one slow breath. The bell holds the time.
A daughter is better. In SN 3.16, King Pasenadi frowns at a daughter's birth, and the Buddha tells him a woman may turn out better than a man, wise and virtuous. Today's word.
Your line: a daughter may be better. When something unexpected lands today, catch the first frown, and give it one breath before you decide what it is. Day six hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite the verse to Pasenadi when discussing the place of women and girls, and many communities read it alongside the nuns' own verses in the Therigatha.

fork.reveal: SN 3.16 has the Buddha speak up right then, to the king himself, naming wisdom and virtue.

original.note: Pali Mallika: jasmine, and the name of Pasenadi's queen, the mother in SN 3.16.

trapdoor: what you thought: a daughter is better is a modern slogan.
what it means: in SN 3.16, the Buddha tells a disappointed king that a woman may turn out better than a man, wise and virtuous.

what a scholar hears: the verse's praise also uses the roles of its age, a wife who honors her mother-in-law and the mother of a ruler; scholars read it as both bold for its court and bounded by its time.
